article.overview: A geophone is a sensor that converts ground movement into an electrical voltage. In lunar work it is usually used as the receiver in an active seismic experiment: a known source, such as a thumper, a mortar or an explosive charge, makes the ground vibrate, and the geophones record how those waves travel through the regolith and crust. Three Apollo missions carried geophone-based experiments: the Active Seismic Experiment (ASE) on Apollo 14 and Apollo 16, and the Lunar Seismic Profiling Experiment (LSPE) on Apollo 17. Two later payloads still in development, the South Pole Seismic Station (SPSS) and the European ECLIPSE concept, are described as including geophone components. Neither has flown, and their status is set out in the examples below.
article.description: A geophone is a spring-mass device. A coil of wire is suspended on a spring inside a permanent magnet. When the ground moves, the magnet and its housing move with it, while the coil tends to stay still because of inertia. The relative motion between coil and magnet induces a voltage in the coil. Above its natural (resonant) frequency, that voltage is proportional to ground velocity, which is why geophones are described as velocity transducers [1][2][9]. Geophones are often confused with seismometers. The Apollo passive seismic experiments (the PSE, LP and SP sensors) were seismometers, not geophones [5]. A review cited by one secondary source gives a usable band of about 1-15 Hz for conventional geophones and describes seismometers as covering a wider band, typically about 0.01 to 50 Hz [9][10]; that review was not read directly. The Apollo LSPE geophones were specified for 2-20 Hz operation [3]. In the Apollo designs the geophone was a passive coil transducer, and the amplification and logarithmic compression of its signal were performed by the ALSEP central station electronics [1][2].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar geophone experiment is active seismic profiling. Because the source is controlled, its time and position are known, so scientists can measure the travel time and amplitude of waves from the source to each geophone and infer the seismic velocities and thicknesses of the layers beneath the site [1][2]. The Apollo 17 LSPE used charges detonated at distances of 100 to 2700 m from the geophone array, and its travel-time data reached about 2.7 km [2]. The Apollo 14 ASE used a thumper and a planned set of mortar shots to provide a local profile beneath the station [1]. A geophone array can also record other sources: the Apollo 17 LSPE recorded signals from the lunar module's ascent stage at ranges of 148, 244, 190 and 187 m from its four geophone sites [2].
article.operating_principle: A moving-coil geophone is a passive transducer. Its output depends on the velocity of the ground relative to the magnet, and it has a natural resonance that sets the frequency at which its response is strongest. The Apollo 14 PSR gives a nominal natural frequency of 7.5 Hz for the ASE geophone [1], and the Apollo 17 PSR gives the same nominal value for the LSPE geophone [2]. The output per unit ground velocity is the generator constant, quoted in V/(m/s); per-unit values are listed in the comparison table below. Each geophone's output passed to the ALSEP central station, where it was amplified and logarithmically compressed before digitisation and telemetry [1][2]. The Apollo 14 PSR gives a digital sampling frequency of 500 Hz [1]; the Apollo 17 PSR gives 118 samples per second per channel with 7-bit log-compressed samples [2]. The Apollo 14 thumper is shown in the operating principle image below [23].

article.scientific_importance: Passive seismometers listen for events that nature produces, such as moonquakes and impacts. Active geophone experiments use a known source to probe the ground beneath a specific site, so the timing of the source is known and layer structure can be measured directly. The Apollo 14 ASE gave a P-wave velocity of 104 m/s for the surface layer, which is interpreted as regolith, and 299 m/s for the material below about 8.5 m depth [1]. The Apollo 17 LSPE PSR interprets a layered model: a first layer at 250 m/s, 248 m thick; a second layer at 1200 m/s, 927 m thick; and about 4000 m/s at the base of the second layer, with a total basalt fill of about 1200 m [2]. These interpretations are not uncontested. Cooper et al. (1974), as summarised by Gangi (1979), proposed a five-layer model with velocities of 100, 327, 495, 960 and 4700 m/s, or alternatively a continuous model V = 395 + 778z (m/s, z in metres) [4]. The LSPE PSR presents a stepwise model [2][4]. The two models differ and this article does not resolve the difference.

physical_specifications.note: There is no single universal specification for a geophone. Geophones are built to suit an experiment's frequency band, sensitivity, deployment method and power budget. Values below apply only to the named instrument and source. Where a value is not published in the sources consulted, it is marked as not publicly specified.

related_non_geophone_instruments: Chandrayaan-3 ILSA (India, flown): ISRO describes a cluster of six high-sensitivity accelerometers, not a geophone [17]. Sensitivity, band, mass and power are not stated on the ISRO page.

Chang'e-7 lunar seismograph (China, planned): described as a broadband and MEMS seismometer [15]. The calibration paper's abstract describes an eight-year design lifetime. Sensor count, band, mass and power are not stated in the abstract. Launch status is unclear: Wikipedia gives 2027 as planned and describes the 2026 window as indefinitely delayed [16].

NASA Lunar Geophysical Network (LGN) concept: the 2020 decadal study describes a broadband seismometer, a short-period seismometer and a Silicon Audio borehole seismometer, and does not identify a geophone [14]. A search-snippet claim that the NASA Silicon Audio instrument combines a geophone and a laser interferometer is not confirmed by the 2020 report and is not used. The report's CBE and MEV mass and power estimates were layout-extracted and are not used here.
NASA LEMS-A3 (Artemis III, in development): described as a three-axis seismometer. Specifications were not extracted from the sources read [18][19].

article.dimensions_and_proportions: The geophone dimensions for the Apollo experiments are not publicly specified in the sources read. The LSPE geophone module, the Apollo 14 and 16 ASE layouts and the SPSS and ECLIPSE concepts describe array geometry rather than geophone size. Array geometry is important: the Apollo 14 ASE spread ran 94 m from the station [1], the Apollo 16 ASE profile was about 90 m [4], and the Apollo 17 LSPE triangle had geophone 2 at 148 m from geophone 1 [2].
article.mass_and_weight: The mass of an individual Apollo geophone is not publicly specified in the sources read, so no geophone mass is given. Wikipedia reports an ASE package mass of 11.2 kg, which is not verified against a primary NASA document and is not used as a geophone value [7]. The SPSS and ECLIPSE geophone masses are not publicly specified [11][13].
article.power_requirements: The Apollo 17 LSPE drew 5.3 W in operating mode, the same regardless of ambient temperature [3]. Wikipedia reports 9.75 W for the ASE package, which is not verified against a primary NASA document [7]. The power requirements of the SPSS and ECLIPSE geophones are not publicly specified [11][13].
article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Geophones must be coupled firmly to the ground, because their response depends on the ground moving the magnet and housing. Tilt is a key requirement: the LSPE data would be lost completely if a geophone was 15 degrees or more from vertical, and a spike must be within 7 degrees of vertical to be effective [3]. In Apollo 14, one geophone was tilted and its effective resonance rose from 7.5 to 13.4 Hz [1]. One geophone was reported to have pulled out of the ground at a thumper position [1]. Movement of the commander near the station disturbed the geophone line during Apollo 14 operations [1]. The Apollo 17 LSPE drew 5.3 W in operating mode [3]. The sources read do not state radiation, vacuum, thermal or micrometeoroid tolerances for the Apollo geophones; those requirements are not publicly specified and are not inferred here.
article.limitations: A geophone's useful band is set by its resonance. The Apollo LSPE's 2-20 Hz band [3] is narrower than the broadband seismometers described for the other lunar payloads discussed here. An active experiment only measures what its source provides: the Apollo 14 ASE had 13 successful thumper shots, and several other positions misfired or were not used [1][7]. Apollo 14 planned four mortar impacts at about 150, 300, 900 and 1500 m, but the PSR text read does not confirm that any were fired [1]. Geophone response depends on alignment; the tilted Apollo 14 geophone shows how alignment changes the response [1]. The Apollo 14 PSR gives 500 Hz sampling [1], while Yamada gives 530 Hz for both Apollo 14 and 16 [5]; both are recorded. The Apollo 17 operating data rate of 3,533 bits/s is not reconciled with the per-channel sampling rate in the sources read [2][3].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A geophone experiment is delivered as part of a larger payload, so its transportation depends on the host system. The Apollo and proposed systems differ considerably, and no lander or spacecraft compatibility is claimed in this article.
transportation_process: Integrate the geophone array and its cabling into the spacecraft payload on Earth.
Launch the payload using a launch vehicle.
Transfer the payload towards the Moon.
Deliver the payload to the surface with a lander.
Deploy the geophones on a stable surface, couple them firmly to the ground and level them.
Connect the array to the central station or host system for power and data, and control the tilt and thermal interfaces.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Deployment methods vary. In the Apollo 14 ASE, the geophones and cables were stowed on the thumper until deployment and then placed by the astronaut [1]. In the Apollo 17 LSPE, the crew deployed the module, four geophones and cable reels [3]. The LSPE geophones were arranged in a triangle with a central geophone, and the module was placed 9 m south of the central station [3].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo missions deployed geophones by astronaut placement as part of their surface experiment packages. The transport to the Moon was part of the Apollo mission architecture and is not described in detail in the sources read. SPSS and ECLIPSE are proposed systems; no verified lander or deployment plan is available in the sources read [11][13].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is claimed. SPSS is selected for development for Artemis IV, with final manifesting not decided [11]. ECLIPSE is a proposed concept submitted to an ESA call [13]. Compatibility would need to be assessed against verified mass, dimensions, mounting, landing loads, deployment, power and data requirements, none of which are publicly specified for the geophones.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo active seismic experiments are the flown lunar geophone experiments documented in the sources read. The Apollo 14 and 16 ASEs and the Apollo 17 LSPE produced P-wave velocity models of the lunar near-surface and crust [1][2][4]. Their results contributed to understanding of regolith and basalt structure beneath the Apollo sites, though the interpretations differ between sources [4]. Later lunar seismic payloads have turned to other designs. SPSS and ECLIPSE both propose geophone components, but neither has flown, and the sources read describe the current lunar seismic programme mostly in terms of broadband and MEMS seismometers [11][13][14][15]. The Apollo passive seismic experiments (PSEs) were seismometers rather than geophones [5]; the Apollo 11 PSE was not checked individually in this run. No Apollo 15 geophone experiment was confirmed in the sources consulted.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Manufacturer, mass, dimensions and operating temperature of the Apollo geophones are not publicly specified in the sources read. Per-unit sensitivity in V/um for the Apollo 14 and 16 ASEs was not found; the generator constants in V/(m/s) are the values available. The Apollo 16 geophone layout is taken from a scanned secondary source [4], and the Apollo 16 and 17 per-unit values are from Yamada [5] rather than the primary PSR text. The Apollo 17 PSR table text is garbled and should be checked against the page image. The Apollo 16 PSR ASE chapter was not read in full [6]. A commonly quoted typical geophone natural frequency of about 10 Hz is not supported by a primary source in the sources read and is not used. A value of 30 V/(m/s) appears on Wikipedia with a 'clarification needed' flag and no source, and is not used [9]. The SPSS geophone claim rests on the CNES/IPGP release alone [12]. The Artemis IV date is not firm. The Chang'e-7 launch status is unclear because the sources conflict [15][16]. Image rights: Apollo images on Wikimedia Commons are described as NASA works in the public domain; the rights statements were not independently verified for each file. The SPSS artwork is credited to NASA/JPL-Caltech; its reuse terms were not checked.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url, source_page_url, source_url, pdf_url and reference url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Direct image URLs were checked with HTTP requests on 2026-11-12: the three Apollo Wikimedia Commons assets and the Active Seismic Experiment thumper PNG returned HTTP 200 with image content types, and the SPSS NASA asset returned HTTP 200 image/jpeg. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. The IBIBLIO Data Book URL contains parentheses, commas and percent-encoded spaces; these are part of the path and were kept unchanged.

data_quality_notes: catalogue_id is set to the catalogue payload ID (5), following the convention used for payloads 002 to 004. The exact catalogue name 'Geophone' and category 1 'Geophysical and lunar interior instruments' were confirmed against lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md.
Output files follow the ledger naming for payload 005 (geophone_payload_005_v1.md and .json) and sit in lunar_payload_explorer/data/payloads/ with the earlier 002 to 004 outputs.
Apollo 14 sampling conflict: the Apollo 14 PSR gives a 500 Hz digital sampling frequency [1]; Yamada gives 530 Hz for Apollo 14 and 16 [5]. Both are recorded and not reconciled.
Apollo 14 quantisation conflict: Gangi (OCR-read) gives 5-bit samples with 0-51 levels [4]; Yamada gives 32 levels [5]. This is not included in the article body; the conflict is recorded here only.

Apollo 14 thumper count conflict: the PSR gives 21 initiator positions and 13 successful shots [1]. Wikipedia gives 22 charges and says 13 of 22 fired with 5 of 18 misfired [7]; that is internally inconsistent and is not used.
Apollo 14 PSR mentions a related 108 m/s value for the Apollo 12 site; this value is not used in the article because it does not refer to the Apollo 14 site.

Apollo 16 geophone layout (three geophones, 150 ft spacing, about 90 m profile) is from Gangi's OCR-read secondary source [4]. The Apollo 16 PSR ASE chapter was not read in full [6]; the Apollo 16 PSR full PDS copy is 743 MB and the NTRS record has no PDF.
Apollo 16 nominal natural frequency is not stated in the primary text read. The per-unit values are from Yamada [5].

Apollo 17 per-unit resonance and generator constants are from Yamada's compilation of PSR Table 10-I [5]. The PSR table text layer is garbled, so these values must be verified on the page image before use.

Apollo 17 data rate conflict: the operating-mode data rate of 3,533 bits/s [3] is not reconciled with 4 channels x 118 samples/s x 7 bits = 3,304 bits/s from the per-channel figures [2]. Both are recorded.
Apollo 17 per-channel sampling: the PSR gives 118 samples per second per channel [2]; Yamada gives 117.78 Hz [5]. The article records the PSR value and the Yamada value.
Apollo 17 LSPE explosive packages: eight packages with charges from 1/8 lb to 6 lb [3], all detonated 15-18 December 1972 [2].

Geophone mass, dimensions and operating temperature are not publicly specified for any Apollo geophone in the sources read. The ASE package mass (11.2 kg) and power (9.75 W) are from Wikipedia only and are not used as geophone values.

Typical geophone natural frequency: the Wikipedia 10 Hz value is unsourced on that page, and the 4-14 Hz range is from an unfetched search summary. Neither is used. The article gives only the Apollo nominal values (7.5 Hz).
Typical geophone sensitivity: the 30 V/(m/s) value on Wikipedia is flagged 'clarification needed' and unsourced. Not used.
Hou et al. (2021) usable band of 1-15 Hz is cited through Wikipedia [9][10] and was not read directly. Treated as a secondary statement.

SPSS geophone claim is single-source: the CNES/IPGP release states three geophones [12]; the NASA/JPL release does not mention geophones [11]. The JPL source page returned HTTP 403 to the checking tool, so the NASA text was read via WebFetch rather than a direct request. The SPSS active source is 'thumper' per NASA [11] and PASS per CNES/IPGP [12]; the identity is not confirmed.

SPSS date conflict: the NASA/JPL dateline is 4 December 2025 [11], which is a publication date, not a launch date. Digital Trends (via search summary) gives September 2028 and a NASA event page (via search summary) gives early 2028; neither was verified in a primary NASA document. The article states that the date is not firm.
ECLIPSE is a conference abstract only [13]; it describes two horizontal geophones and one vertical short-period geophone. Specifications are not publicly specified in the abstract.

Chang'e-7: the abstract gives keywords 'broadband seismometer' and 'MEMS seismometer' and an eight-year design lifetime [15]. The two three-axis, six-channel description comes from a search summary and was not verified in the full text, so it is not used. Launch date conflicts: Wikipedia gives 2027 as planned and describes the 2026 window as indefinitely delayed [16]; other sources were not verified.
Chang'e-7 payload count: Wikipedia gives 21 science payloads (six international) and another source gives 23 (seven international). The conflict is unresolved and the count is not used.

LGN: the 2020 report describes seismometers and does not identify a geophone [14]. The search-summary claim that the NASA Silicon Audio instrument combines a geophone and a laser interferometer is not confirmed by the report and is not used. Layout-extracted CBE and MEV mass and power values from Table 4 are not used.
LEMS-A3 (Artemis III): the NASA project page was read as a search snippet only [19]; the ICES-2025 paper [18] was not readable for seismometer specifications. No LEMS specifications are given.
ILSA (Chandrayaan-3): ISRO describes six high-sensitivity accelerometers [17], not geophones. ILSA is listed as a related instrument only; it is not compared as a geophone.
Apollo 11 PSE was not checked individually in this run; the statement that the Apollo PSEs were seismometers relies on Yamada [5] and the Apollo 14 PSR [1].
Apollo 15: no geophone experiment is confirmed in the sources consulted.

Images excluded: a Commons photograph of the Apollo 17 LSPE transmitter antenna (AS17-136-20704) was reviewed and excluded because it does not depict geophones. A Commons LSPE explosive-charge diagram (GIF) was not included because its credit was not verified and the Commons page was not read.

NASA-hosted image copies (images-assets.nasa.gov and spaceflight.nasa.gov) for AS14-67-9361, AS16-113-18377 and two AS17 images returned HTTP 403 to the checking tool. Wikimedia Commons copies were used instead and verified with HTTP 200.

The Commons photograph AS14-67-9374 is described on Commons as showing the geophone line being laid out; the PSR figure caption (as cited on Commons) describes firing the thumper along the line. The article uses the Commons caption wording and notes the difference.

Image rights: Apollo images on Wikimedia Commons are recorded as NASA works in the public domain; rights statements were not independently verified for each file. SPSS artwork is credited to NASA/JPL-Caltech; its reuse terms were not checked.
